claim: A simulated radar caught 99 % of falls but raised 51 false alarms a day, far too many.
data_label: simulated data: 60 GHz FMCW radar model, seeded
stats: false alarms, from 17 in 8 h simulated
limit: Simulation only, and the false-alarm rate is unusable; no real radar or people; not a medical device.
alt: Two spectrogram panels with speed on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. In the top panel a short bright burst at a fast downward speed is followed by stillness and a red alarm line; the height line drops to the floor. In the bottom panel sitting down gives a similar burst but the height stays at seat level and there is no alarm.
post:
Falls are a leading reason older people lose their independence, and the usual answers are a camera (privacy problem) or a wearable (often not worn).

I built an open-source research demo of a third option: a 60 GHz FMCW radar that sees motion, not faces. It is a simulation of the whole chain: a moving point-scatterer body, radar signal synthesis with room clutter and multipath, range and Doppler FFTs, micro-Doppler features, a 7.2 KB ONNX classifier plus a rule-based check, a confirmation window and a cancel option. Only a few derived numbers leave the device as MQTT JSON, which fits the Swiss nFADP privacy idea.

Measured on simulated data: 207 of 210 falls alarmed (99 %), 17 false alarms in 8 hours of daily living (51.0 per day extrapolated), median 8 s from impact to alarm including the confirmation wait. Sitting down fast and lying on a bed were part of the 239 fall-like events. That false-alarm rate is far too high for real use.

What is not verified: everything here is simulated. No real radar, no real people, no care-home trial. It is a research demo, not a medical device.

What would you check first before trusting a system like this near a person who lives alone?

Code: https://github.com/VB-Builds/radar-fall-detector
